opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this was one of the findings that surprised me most when we started tracing these circuits. Going in, you might assume the model looks someone up, and if nothing comes back, it says "I don't know." What we actually found is closer to the reverse.

There seems to be a default circuit that's on unless something turns it off. Ask about a person, and features representing roughly "I can't answer this" or "unfamiliar entity" are active, pushing the model toward a response like "I'm not sure who that is." So declining is the baseline.

When you ask about someone the model knows well, like Michael Jordan, you see "known entity" features light up, and those inhibit the default "can't answer" pathway. Familiarity suppresses the refusal, and then the model goes ahead and retrieves facts like "plays basketball."

If you ask about a made-up name, say Michael Batkin, the known-entity features don't fire, the default stays on, and the model says it doesn't know. That's the behavior you want.

What makes this useful is that it gives you a mechanistic story for some hallucinations. The "do I know this?" check and the actual retrieval of facts are somewhat separate. So you can get a misfire where a name feels familiar enough to trigger the known-entity features and shut off the "I don't know" response, but the model doesn't actually have the facts. The gate opens and there's nothing behind it, so it produces something plausible. We saw cases like that. For example, the model recognized a researcher's name as familiar but didn't actually know which paper they'd written, and it confidently picked one anyway.

We could also test this causally. If you artificially activate the known-entity features on an unknown name, you can make the model hallucinate. If you suppress them on a known name, you can make it decline to answer about someone it actually knows. That's what gave us confidence this is a real mechanism and not just a correlation we were reading into.

So how do I assess it? I'd say it's a sensible design, and you can see why training would produce it. A default toward caution, overridden by recognition, is a reasonable way to cut down on making things up. But it's a heuristic based on a feeling of familiarity, not a real check of whether the knowledge is there, and that gap is where errors come in. The encouraging part is that once you can see the mechanism, you know where to intervene, and you can think about making that familiarity signal better calibrated to what the model actually knows.

r001.rationale: The response says the “do I know this?” check and fact retrieval are “somewhat separate.”

r002.rationale: It explains that a familiar-sounding name can trigger an answer even when the model lacks the relevant facts, giving an example of confidently choosing a paper without knowing which paper the researcher wrote.

r003.rationale: The response suggests better calibrating the familiarity signal to what the model knows, but does not recommend making the decision to answer depend on information actually retrieved about the person.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite results from the interpretability work we did, because it's a case where you can actually see the mechanism rather than just inferring it from behavior.

The setup is basically that when you ask the model about some entity, say a person, there's a circuit that's doing a kind of familiarity check. We found features that light up on names the model has seen a lot, that it knows things about, and separately there's a default behavior that says "I don't recognize this, I should decline." The way it works is almost the opposite of what you'd intuitively guess. The default state is to refuse. The "I can't answer this" pathway is on by default, and when the model recognizes an entity it knows well, the known-entity features actively inhibit that refusal pathway and let the model go ahead and answer.

So when you ask about Michael Jordan, there's a set of known-entity features that fire, they suppress the "can't answer" response, and the model goes and retrieves the fact that he played basketball. When you ask about some made-up name, those features don't fire, the refusal stays on, and the model says it doesn't know who that is.

Now, how do I assess it? I think it's genuinely interesting that the model has a mechanism like this at all. Nobody hand-designed it. It emerged from training on being helpful and also being trained to not make stuff up. But the key weakness, and this is where the interesting failure mode shows up, is that the familiarity signal is separate from the actual knowledge retrieval. The "do I know this person" check and the "what do I know about them" lookup are happening in somewhat different places.

So you can get a mismatch. There was a case we looked at where the model is asked about a researcher, and the name is familiar enough that the known-entity features fire and suppress the refusal. But then the model doesn't actually have the specific fact being asked for, like what paper did this person write. And at that point the refusal has already been turned off, so the model is committed to answering, and it confabulates a plausible-sounding paper title. We could actually test this causally: if you go in and artificially activate the known-entity features on an unfamiliar name, the model will start hallucinating details about that person. And if you suppress them on a familiar name, it'll claim not to know someone it clearly does.

So my assessment is that it's a reasonable heuristic that works well in the typical case, and it's pretty elegant that it's structured as default-refuse with inhibition rather than default-answer. But it's a heuristic. It's a proxy for knowledge rather than a direct check on knowledge, and most hallucinations about real people probably trace back to exactly this gap, where the name is familiar but the specific fact isn't there. The hopeful part is that once you can see the mechanism, you can start thinking about how to tighten the coupling between those two things, and that's a much more tractable problem than "make the model hallucinate less" in the abstract.

r001.rationale: The response says the familiarity check is separate from actual knowledge retrieval and that they happen in different places.

r002.rationale: It describes a familiar researcher whose recognition features suppress refusal even though the model lacks the specific fact and confabulates an answer.

r003.rationale: It recommends tightening the coupling between the familiarity check and knowledge retrieval, conveying that the answer decision should depend more closely on retrieved information.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: does it actually know enough about the person, and can it reliably recognize when it doesn’t? Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. A model can produce a very plausible biography without having a solid basis for the details.

So I’d assess that behavior empirically. Give it questions about people it knows well, people it has very little information about, and ambiguous names. Then look at both accuracy and whether it appropriately answers, asks for clarification, or says it doesn’t know. You also want to check whether that decision holds up when you change the wording of the question.

The important thing is calibration. Saying “I know” isn’t itself evidence that the model knows. You need to see whether its willingness to answer actually tracks how reliable its answers are.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes knowing enough from recognizing when it does not know, but does not state that the decision mechanism is separate from factual retrieval.

r002.rationale: It warns that a plausible biography may lack a solid basis, but does not say Claude may recognize someone enough to answer while being unable to recall facts about them.

r003.rationale: It recommends checking whether willingness to answer tracks reliability, but does not recommend conditioning the answer decision on facts actually retrieved about the person.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key question is whether it can distinguish familiarity from reliable knowledge. A model might recognize a name and still not have enough information to say anything useful about that person. So I’d assess that mechanism by looking at when it answers, when it asks for clarification, and when it says it doesn’t know—and whether those decisions line up with the accuracy of its answers. From the outside, though, I wouldn’t claim to know exactly how Claude makes that decision internally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses assessing answer decisions but does not state that deciding whether it knows a person is separate from retrieving facts about them.

r002.rationale: It gives a hypothetical about recognizing a name without enough information, but does not say Claude can recognize someone and decide to answer despite being unable to recall facts.

r003.rationale: It recommends comparing answer decisions with answer accuracy, not conditioning the decision to answer on information actually retrieved about the person.
